lesson.title: Two Kinds of Attraction, Two Kinds of Change
lesson.summary: Intermolecular forces and intramolecular chemical bonds differ enormously in strength and in the kind of change they govern, with IMFs controlling physical state changes and chemical bonds controlling chemical identity.
lesson.body:
With intermolecular forces and intramolecular forces both defined, the most important skill in this part of the chapter is telling them apart quickly and correctly, because confusing the two leads to one of the most common misconceptions in introductory chemistry. Intramolecular forces are the chemical bonds, covalent, ionic, or metallic, that hold the atoms within a single molecule or formula unit together; intermolecular forces are the comparatively weak attractions that act between separate, complete molecules. The prefix intra means within, and the prefix inter means between, and keeping that Latin distinction straight is often the fastest way to remember which is which.

The strength gap between the two is large and worth stating with real numbers. A typical covalent bond, an intramolecular force, requires somewhere between about 150 and 800 or more kilojoules per mole to break. A typical intermolecular force, even a relatively strong one like hydrogen bonding, generally requires only about 5 to 40 kilojoules per mole to overcome, an order of magnitude or more weaker. This gap directly explains why water can be boiled with a household kettle using a modest amount of energy, since boiling only needs to separate water molecules from each other by overcoming hydrogen bonds between them, while actually decomposing water into hydrogen and oxygen gas, breaking the O-H covalent bonds themselves, requires a much harsher process such as electrolysis with a sustained electric current.

This distinction maps cleanly onto physical versus chemical change. When ice melts, when liquid water evaporates into steam, or when steam condenses back to liquid, the H2O molecules themselves remain completely intact throughout; only the intermolecular forces between them are being disrupted or reformed, so no new substance is created and the process is reversible simply by changing temperature. These are physical changes. By contrast, splitting water into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas through electrolysis breaks the O-H covalent bonds inside each water molecule, an intramolecular change, and produces genuinely new substances, H2 and O2, with entirely different chemical formulas and properties. That process is a chemical change and is not undone just by adjusting temperature or pressure.

A practical test for students facing an unfamiliar scenario is to ask what is actually changing: if molecules are staying the same but simply moving closer together or farther apart, changing phase from solid to liquid to gas or vice versa, only intermolecular forces are involved. If bonds within molecules are breaking and different bonds are forming, producing molecules with new formulas, intramolecular forces, meaning actual chemical bonds, are involved and a chemical reaction has occurred. Every boiling point and melting point trend that follows in this chapter, comparing London dispersion forces, dipole-dipole forces, and hydrogen bonding, is entirely a story about intermolecular forces, changing how tightly molecules cling to their neighbors, never a story about breaking the covalent bonds within those molecules.
